newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lower rates wouldn't solve jobs problem - Stark. [CORRECTED 16:17 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Lower rates wouldn't solve jobs problem - Stark. [CORRECTED 16:17 GMT]

text.p: Germany's finance ministry does not believe lower interest rates would solve Europe's structural economic problems, including high unemployment, state secretary Juergen Stark said on Monday.

"Further interest rate cuts would do absolutely nothing to solve our structural problems. Nor would an increase in public deficits stimulate private-sector demand," he said after a meeting of EU finance ministers, which he attended in Finance Minister Theo Waigel's stead.
Interest rates in Europe have already reached the lowest levels in 30 to 40 years, but growth and investment remain sluggish.

One reason for the low level of German investment, often cited as the main factor behind the disappointing weakness of the past year's economic rebound, is that capacity utilisation remains low, Stark said.

Only policies that directly address structural issues such as high taxes and non-wage labour costs will help stimulate growth and create jobs, and EU members will have to work on coordinating policiies in these areas across the continent, he said.

Germany's 1996 economic growth of 1.4 percent (corrects from 1.9 percent) was better than interim projections, and the government stands by its expectation of a rebound to 2.5 percent growth this year, fueled by exports, low interest rates and stable prices.
The recent correction of the dollar's previous undervaluation has also been a positive factor, he said.
